title: How Thinking About Bilingual Children Changed
text:
For much of the twentieth century, schools in several countries advised immigrant parents to speak only the majority language at home. Bilingual children were scoring lower on verbal tests, and the conclusion drawn was that two languages crowded one another out of a limited space. Those studies were badly confounded. The bilingual children were usually poorer, they were often tested in their weaker language, and sometimes they were tested by people they could barely understand. When such factors were controlled, most of the supposed deficit disappeared.

What replaced that picture is more interesting than a simple reversal. Evidence from reaction times and eye movements suggests that both languages stay active even when only one is in use, so a bilingual speaker is continually selecting one and suppressing the other. Code-switching, once dismissed as confusion, turns out to be rule-governed: speakers switch at predictable grammatical boundaries and for identifiable social reasons. Whether all that practice in selection produces a general advantage in attention is still disputed, and several early findings have proved hard to replicate. The educational point, though, is not disputed. A child's home language is a resource, and programmes that build literacy in it tend to improve outcomes in the second language rather than harm them.
points: Schools once told immigrant families to use only the majority language because bilingual children scored lower.
Those studies were confounded by poverty and by testing children in their weaker language.
Both languages stay active in a bilingual speaker, who constantly selects one and suppresses the other.
Code-switching follows grammatical and social rules rather than showing confusion.
A general cognitive advantage from bilingualism is disputed and hard to replicate.
Building literacy in the home language improves rather than harms the second language.
